questions.q: In computing, 'data' is best defined as:
o: any raw fact, observation, or measurement that can be recorded
the final report produced after analysis
only numbers stored in a database
questions.e: Data is any raw fact, observation, or measurement that can be recorded (numbers, text, images, audio, video, sensor readings, logs, clicks); it is the raw material we process, analyze and interpret to extract meaning.

questions.q: Regarding data architecture, traditional data typically uses a ______, whereas big data uses a ______.
questions.e: Traditional data uses a centralized database (all data in one place, e.g. SQL Server), while big data uses a distributed database (data spread across many servers, e.g. Facebook across global servers).

questions.q: In terms of data types, traditional data is mainly ______, while big data is mainly ______.
o: structured (tables, rows, columns); unstructured and semi-structured
questions.e: Traditional data is structured (tables, rows, columns, e.g. an Excel sheet of customers), while big data is unstructured and semi-structured (e.g. tweets, YouTube videos with comments, IoT sensor data).

questions.q: Regarding schema, the difference between traditional data and big data is that:
o: traditional data uses a fixed schema (defined before storing); big data uses a dynamic schema (store first, organize later)
big data defines schema before storing
questions.e: Traditional data has a fixed schema (structure defined before storing, e.g. a bank DB always has Account Number, Balance, Holder Name), while big data has a dynamic schema — store first, organize later.

questions.q: Traditional data typically scales using ______, whereas big data scales using ______.
o: vertical scaling (bigger servers); horizontal scaling (many small servers)
questions.e: Traditional data needs bigger servers (vertical scaling, e.g. upgrading SQL server hardware), while big data scales with many small servers (horizontal scaling, e.g. Netflix using thousands of distributed servers).

questions.q: Data Analytics is best described as:
o: looking at data carefully to find useful information, patterns, and insights that help make better decisions
questions.e: Data Analytics means looking at data carefully to find useful information, patterns and insights that can help in making better decisions — the process of collecting, checking and learning from data.

questions.q: The four types of data analytics, in order of increasing value and difficulty, are:
questions.e: The four types are Descriptive (what happened?), Diagnostic (why did it happen?), Predictive (what will happen?), and Prescriptive (what should we do?); the level of insight and value increases from step 1 to 4.

questions.q: Descriptive analytics answers which question?
questions.e: Descriptive analytics answers 'What happened?' — e.g. 'Last month, you sold 500 juices.'

questions.q: Diagnostic analytics answers which question?
questions.e: Diagnostic analytics answers 'Why did it happen?' — e.g. 'Sales dropped on rainy days because fewer people came outside.'

questions.q: Predictive analytics answers which question?
questions.e: Predictive analytics answers 'What will happen?' — e.g. 'Next summer, mango juice sales will increase by 30%.'

questions.q: Prescriptive analytics answers which question?
o: What should we do (and how to make it happen)?
questions.e: Prescriptive analytics answers 'What should we do?' — e.g. 'Keep extra mangoes in stock for summer weekends.'

questions.q: Compared with traditional data, big data is described as giving results that are:
o: highly accurate, because it analyzes all types of data
less accurate, limited by schema and size
questions.e: Traditional data gives less accurate results (limited by schema and size), while big data gives highly accurate results because it analyzes all types of data (e.g. Amazon predicting purchases using browsing and purchase history).

questions.q: In terms of volume, traditional data is typically measured in ______, while big data is measured in ______.
questions.e: Traditional data involves a small amount of data (Gigabytes–Terabytes), while big data involves very large data (Petabytes or more, e.g. Google processing petabytes of search queries daily).

questions.q: Why is exploring relationships harder in big data than in traditional data?
o: the data is huge and messy, unlike traditional data where joins and foreign keys make relationships easy
questions.e: In traditional data, relationships are easy to explore (joins, foreign keys); in big data, relationships are hard to explore because the data is huge and messy (e.g. finding links between millions of tweets and COVID-19 spread).

questions.q: Which is a real-world example of data analytics given in the material?
questions.e: Real-world examples include Netflix using data analytics to recommend movies/shows, banks detecting unusual (fraudulent) transactions, and hospitals predicting disease risks from patient history.

questions.q: Why is data considered so important today ('the new oil')?
o: it drives decision-making, generates revenue through insights, and powers AI/ML
questions.e: Data drives decision-making (companies use data instead of guessing), equals money/the new oil (businesses earn by analyzing and selling insights), and powers automation and AI (ML/DL become powerful because of lots of data).

questions.q: Big data analytics can be divided into which two major sub-systems?
questions.e: Big data analytics is a method to uncover hidden patterns in large data and extract useful information; it can be divided into two major sub-systems: data management and analysis.

questions.q: Batch processing is best described as processing data:
o: that is collected and stored first, then analyzed later in bulk
as soon as it is created
questions.e: Batch processing (data at rest) means you collect data first, store it, then analyze it later in bulk; it is useful when accuracy matters more than speed. Tools include Hadoop and Spark (batch mode).

questions.q: Stream processing is best described as processing data:
o: as soon as it is created (in motion), when immediate action is needed
only when the server is idle
questions.e: Stream processing (data in motion) means processing and analyzing data as soon as it is created; it is useful when immediate action is needed. Tools include Apache Storm, Apache Kafka and Spark Streaming.

questions.q: A bank's fraud detection system that blocks a suspicious transaction in seconds is an example of:
questions.e: A fraud detection system that detects and blocks a suspicious transaction the moment it happens (in seconds) is an example of stream processing (data in motion), where immediate action is needed.

questions.q: An e-commerce site that stores all daily sales data and analyzes it overnight to find top products is an example of:
questions.e: Storing all daily sales and running analysis at night (where it doesn't matter if results take 1–2 hours) is batch processing — data at rest, where accuracy matters more than speed.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches processing type to its data state?
o: batch = data in motion; stream = data at rest
batch = data at rest; stream = data in motion
questions.e: Big data technologies divide into batch processing (analytics on data at rest) and stream processing (analytics on data in motion).

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a tool for batch processing?
questions.e: Batch processing tools include Hadoop and Spark (batch mode); Apache Storm, Apache Kafka and Spark Streaming are listed for stream processing.

questions.q: Which is a positive business-related outcome of big data analytics named in the material?
o: new revenue opportunities and competitive advantages over rivals
questions.e: Big data analytics can lead to positive outcomes: new revenue opportunities, more effective marketing, better customer service, improved operational efficiency, and competitive advantages over rivals.

questions.q: Which of the following is a software/analytics process used in big data analytics?
o: data mining, which sifts through data sets in search of patterns and relationships
questions.e: Big data analytics uses tools for data mining (search for patterns/relationships), predictive analytics (forecast models), machine learning (algorithms on large data), and deep learning (an advanced offshoot of ML).

questions.q: Deep learning is described as:
o: a more advanced offshoot of machine learning
questions.e: Deep learning is described as a more advanced offshoot of machine learning, which taps algorithms to analyze large data sets.

questions.q: How does big data analytics differ from traditional data analytics in the 'what people eat' example?
o: traditional analyzes a small sample (e.g. 100 people); big data analyzes millions of records (bills, orders, apps) for a deeper, more accurate picture
questions.e: Traditional data analytics = asking 100 people and analyzing; big data analytics = analyzing millions of supermarket bills, restaurant orders and delivery-app data, giving a much deeper and more accurate picture.

questions.q: Netflix/YouTube using big data analytics primarily to recommend content works by:
o: analyzing millions of videos watched and recommending based on your history plus what similar users watch
questions.e: Netflix/YouTube analyze millions of videos watched daily and recommend movies/shows based on your history plus what millions of others like you watch.

questions.q: In the evolution of data, relational database management systems (RDBMS) that enabled structured storage in tables emerged in the:
questions.e: In the 1970s and 1980s, the development of RDBMS revolutionized data storage, allowing structured storage using tables; data warehousing emerged in the 1990s, and cloud computing in the 2000s.

questions.q: The concept of data warehousing, which consolidates data from various sources into a single repository, emerged in the:
questions.e: In the 1990s, data warehousing emerged, allowing organizations to consolidate and centralize data from various sources into a single repository, providing a unified view for analysis.

questions.q: GDPR and CCPA are examples of:
o: data privacy regulations that set rules on how companies collect, store and use personal data
questions.e: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) and CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act) are data privacy regulations that set rules on how companies collect, store and use people's personal data.

questions.q: Big Data is defined as data that is:
o: too large, too fast, or too complex for normal databases (like Excel or SQL) to handle
easy for traditional tools to process
questions.e: Big Data means data that is too large, too fast, or too complex for normal databases (like Excel or SQL) to handle — not just lots of data, but also different types from many sources.

questions.q: A common formal definition describes big data as high-volume, high-velocity and high-variety information assets that demand:
o: cost-effective, innovative forms of information processing for enhanced insight and decision making
questions.e: Big data is 'high-volume, high-velocity and high-variety information assets that demand cost-effective, innovative forms of information processing for enhanced insight and decision making.'

questions.q: The five V's of Big Data are:
questions.e: The five V's of Big Data are Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity and Value.

questions.q: In the V's of big data, 'Velocity' refers to:
o: the speed at which data is generated, collected and processed (often in real time)
questions.e: Velocity represents the speed at which data is generated, collected and processed in real-time or near real-time; big data often involves high-velocity streams requiring rapid ingestion and analysis.

questions.q: In the V's of big data, 'Variety' refers to:
o: the diverse range of data types and formats (structured, unstructured, semi-structured)
questions.e: Variety encompasses the diverse range of data types and formats: structured (relational DBs), unstructured (text, images, videos) and semi-structured (JSON, XML).

questions.q: In the V's of big data, 'Veracity' refers to:
o: the quality, reliability and trustworthiness of the data
questions.e: Veracity refers to the quality, reliability and trustworthiness of data; big data often deals with noisy, incomplete or inconsistent data, so ensuring veracity addresses accuracy, integrity and reliability.

questions.q: In the V's of big data, 'Value' refers to:
o: the physical size of the data
deriving actionable insights, intelligence and business value from large, diverse datasets
questions.e: Value represents the ultimate goal of big data: deriving actionable insights, intelligence and business value — identifying patterns, trends, correlations and anomalies that drive innovation and better decisions.

questions.q: A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is especially well-suited for data work because it:
o: handles parallel computing tasks, accelerating data-intensive applications like machine learning
questions.e: GPUs are specialized processors designed to handle parallel computing tasks, making them well-suited for data-intensive applications like machine learning, data visualization and scientific computing with large datasets.

questions.q: RAM (Random Access Memory) is used for:
o: temporarily storing data actively being used or processed by the CPU
questions.e: RAM is a type of computer memory used for temporarily storing data that is actively being used or processed by the CPU; adequate RAM is essential for handling large datasets smoothly.

questions.q: Which of the following are listed as distributed data processing frameworks for big data?
o: Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark and Apache Flink
questions.e: Data processing frameworks such as Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark and Apache Flink provide scalable, distributed computing for processing large datasets across clusters, supporting batch, stream and real-time processing.

questions.q: Which of the following are listed as data visualization tools?
questions.e: Data visualization tools such as Tableau, Power BI and matplotlib (a Python library) let users create interactive, visually appealing representations of data.

questions.q: The main focus of big data technologies is to:
o: require a supercomputer for every task
make computations on big data feasible without a supercomputer, using clusters of commodity hardware
store data on a single machine
questions.e: Big data technologies focus on discovering patterns in semi/unstructured data and making computations feasible without a supercomputer, using clusters of commodity hardware.

questions.q: According to the material, Facebook generates approximately how much data per day?
questions.e: Facebook generates about 4 Petabytes of data per day — that's a million Gigabytes.

questions.q: Collaborative filtering (used in recommendation systems) recommends items based on:
o: the preferences and behavior of similar users, not the item attributes
the attributes/characteristics of the items themselves
questions.e: Collaborative filtering recommends items based on the preferences and behavior of similar users; it does not rely on the characteristics or attributes of the items themselves — if two users liked similar items before, they likely will again.

questions.q: Content-based filtering recommends items based on:
o: the attributes/characteristics of the items plus the user's own past preferences
the behavior of other similar users
questions.e: Content-based filtering recommends items based on the attributes or characteristics of the items themselves, together with the user's past preferences/behavior, recommending items similar to those the user liked before.

questions.q: 'Expertise location' as a big data use case means:
o: analyzing employee profiles, project histories and skills to identify experts for a task
finding the location of data centers
questions.e: Expertise location analyzes structured/unstructured data (employee profiles, project histories, skill sets) to identify experts based on past experience and knowledge, enabling efficient collaboration and team formation.

questions.q: Which is a stated challenge/problem with big data?
o: big data has no privacy concerns
data quality — big data comes from varied sources and may be heterogeneous, incomplete, or contain errors
questions.e: Problems with big data include data quality (heterogeneous, incomplete, error-prone data), data privacy and security, storage and management, integration/compatibility, processing, governance, scalability, and ethical concerns.

questions.q: According to the material, roughly how much data do we create every day?
questions.e: Every day we create about 2.5 quintillion bytes of data, and 90% of the data in the world has been created in the last two years alone.

questions.q: The three core 'problems with big data' identified are storing growing datasets, handling different data types, and:
o: processing data faster (since disk I/O is expensive and bringing huge data to the computation unit causes bottlenecks)
questions.e: The three problems are: (1) storing exponentially growing datasets, (2) different types of data, and (3) processing data faster — disk I/O operations are inherently expensive, and bringing huge amounts of data to the computation unit causes bottlenecks.

questions.q: A major data privacy and security concern with big data is that:
o: there is no sensitive data in big data
with vast amounts of personal/sensitive data, unauthorized access, breaches and privacy violations can have legal, ethical and reputational consequences
data cannot be accessed by anyone
questions.e: With vast amounts of personal and sensitive information in big data systems, ensuring privacy and security is a major concern; unauthorized access, data breaches and privacy violations can have serious legal, ethical and reputational consequences.

questions.q: 'Data monopolies and inequality' as a big data problem refers to:
o: too many small companies owning data
the concentration of big data in a few large companies, creating monopolies and worsening inequality in access to data and innovation
questions.e: The concentration of big data in the hands of a few large companies can create data monopolies and exacerbate inequalities in access to data and opportunities for innovation; promoting equitable access fosters innovation and competition.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a big data application use case?
questions.e: Named big data application use cases include expertise location, recommendation, commerce, financial analysis, social media monitoring, fraud detection, cybersecurity, genomic medicine, traffic navigation and anomaly detection, among others.

questions.q: Big data transforms financial analysis by:
o: providing real-time insights into market trends, investment opportunities and risk factors, and enabling fraud detection and algorithmic trading
questions.e: Big data transforms financial analysis by providing real-time insights into market trends, investment opportunities and risk factors; it also enables fraud detection, regulatory compliance and algorithmic trading.

questions.q: In commerce, big data primarily helps organizations to:
o: gain deep insights into customer behavior, preferences and purchasing patterns to optimize pricing, offerings and marketing
questions.e: Big data revolutionizes commerce by giving deep insights into customer behavior, preferences and purchasing patterns, letting businesses optimize pricing, product offerings and marketing to target the right customers with the right products at the right time.

questions.q: 'Scalability and performance' is a big data challenge because big data systems must:
o: scale to handle increasing volumes of data and growing numbers of users/applications while staying reliable under high load
questions.e: Big data systems need to scale to handle increasing data volumes and growing numbers of users and applications; ensuring scalability, reliability and performance under high load requires careful system design and optimization.

questions.q: Apache Hadoop is best described as:
o: a collection of open-source software utilities that use a cluster of computers to solve problems involving massive data and computation
questions.e: Apache Hadoop is a collection of open-source software utilities that facilitate using a cluster of computers to solve problems involving massive amounts of data and computation — providing both storage and processing.

questions.q: The two core components of Apache Hadoop are:
questions.e: Hadoop provides storage via HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) and processing via MapReduce, a processing engine that performs calculations and analysis on data stored in HDFS.

questions.q: HDFS stands for:
questions.e: HDFS stands for Hadoop Distributed File System, a multi-machine file system that manages how data is stored and accessed across the nodes, making the system reliable and fault-tolerant.

questions.q: HDFS follows a master-slave architecture in which the master is the ______ and the slaves are the ______.
questions.e: HDFS follows a master-slave architecture: the master node (NameNode) keeps track of where each block of data is stored and manages the namespace; the slave nodes (DataNodes) store the actual data blocks on commodity hardware.

questions.q: The NameNode in HDFS is responsible for:
o: managing the file system namespace and metadata (which blocks are stored on which DataNodes)
questions.e: The NameNode is the master of HDFS; it manages the file system namespace and stores metadata — file names, locations, permissions, and which blocks are stored on which DataNodes. It does not store the actual data.

questions.q: In HDFS, the default replication factor (number of copies of each data block) is typically:
questions.e: HDFS typically makes three copies of each piece of data and stores them on different nodes, so that if one node fails, the data is still available on other nodes.

questions.q: HDFS breaks files into smaller pieces called 'blocks', which are typically sized at:
questions.e: HDFS breaks data into blocks, typically 128 MB or 256 MB in size (far larger than the 4 KB default of Linux), reflecting Hadoop's petabyte scale; these blocks are distributed and replicated across DataNodes.

questions.q: HDFS assumes which data access model for files?
questions.e: HDFS assumes a Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) access model: a file once created, written and closed need not be changed; also, no schema validation is done while dumping data.

questions.q: HDFS closely follows the design of which system?
questions.e: HDFS closely follows the design of the Google File System (GFS); it is designed to reliably store very large files across machines in a large cluster of inexpensive commodity hardware.

questions.q: Rack Awareness in HDFS means that:
o: all data is stored on one rack
Hadoop knows which rack each server is in and places replicas smartly across different racks for fault tolerance
Hadoop ignores where servers are located
questions.e: Rack Awareness means Hadoop knows where each server is located (which rack); when storing replicas, it uses this knowledge to place copies across different racks, improving fault tolerance and data locality.

questions.q: In HDFS rack-aware replica placement, the typical placement of the three replicas is:
o: 1st on the local node, 2nd on another node in the same rack, 3rd on a node in a different rack
all three on the same node
questions.e: Typical placement: the first copy is on the local node (fastest), the second on another server in the same rack (fast local switch), and the third on a server in a different rack (for safety). This balances speed and reliability.

questions.q: In the NameNode, FsImage and EditLog respectively represent:
o: a backup node; a log file
a snapshot of the entire file-system metadata; a record of all recent changes made to the file system
questions.e: FsImage is a snapshot of the entire file-system metadata (directory structure, permissions, block locations), while the EditLog records all recent changes (creating, deleting, renaming files) made after the last snapshot.

questions.q: The main role of the Secondary NameNode is:
o: checkpointing — periodically merging FsImage and EditLog to create a new updated FsImage, keeping the EditLog small
to act as a hot standby/backup for the NameNode
questions.e: The Secondary NameNode is a helper node (NOT a backup/hot standby); its main task is checkpointing — periodically merging FsImage and EditLog to create a new updated FsImage, which keeps the EditLog small and manageable and speeds up NameNode restarts.

questions.q: Why is checkpointing important in HDFS?
o: it prevents the EditLog from growing too big, enabling faster NameNode restart and keeping metadata manageable
questions.e: Checkpointing prevents the EditLog from growing too big (large EditLogs slow down recovery), enables faster NameNode restart (fewer logs to replay) and improves reliability by keeping metadata manageable.

questions.q: A key design assumption of HDFS, given that it runs on inexpensive commodity hardware, is that:
o: only one node is ever used
hardware failure is common, so constant monitoring, error detection, fault tolerance and automatic recovery must be integral to the file system
questions.e: An HDFS instance may consist of thousands of inexpensive commodity nodes that often fail, so some components are virtually non-functional at any time; fault tolerance, error detection, constant monitoring and automatic recovery are integral to the file system.

questions.q: Scanning 100 TB on a single node at 100 MB/s takes about 12 days, but on a 1000-node cluster it takes only about:
questions.e: Scanning 100 TB on 1 node at 100 MB/s = 12 days, but scanning on a 1000-node cluster = about 16 minutes — illustrating the scalability benefit of parallelism across a cluster.

questions.q: To overcome the limited bandwidth of a commodity network, Hadoop's key strategy is to:
o: push computation to the data (run analysis where the data is stored) instead of moving data to a central server
questions.e: Because commodity networks have low bandwidth, the solution is to push computation to the data — send computational tasks to where the data is stored, rather than moving large amounts of data over the network.

questions.q: The mean time between failures (MTBF) illustrates that:
o: with 1 node MTBF is ~3 years, but with 1000 nodes MTBF is ~1 day, so fault tolerance must be built into the storage infrastructure
questions.e: MTBF for 1 node = 3 years, but for 1000 nodes = 1 day; cheap nodes fail, especially many of them, so the solution is to build fault tolerance into the storage infrastructure by replicating files multiple times.

questions.q: A data-parallel programming model (like MapReduce) helps with distributed systems by:
o: forcing users to manage all machines manually
letting users focus only on application development, while the system handles work distribution and fault tolerance
questions.e: Programming distributed systems is hard; a data-parallel programming model limits the user's concern to application development, while the system automatically handles work distribution and fault tolerance.

questions.q: HDFS allows storing which kinds of data?
o: structured, semi-structured and unstructured data (no schema validation while dumping)
questions.e: HDFS allows storing any kind of data — structured, semi-structured and unstructured — following a Write-Once-Read-Many model with no schema validation done while dumping data (store first, organize later).

questions.q: Apache Hadoop is described as the de facto:
o: distributed data operating system for managing resources, data and computing tasks on a cluster
questions.e: Big data needs distributed parallel computing on a cluster; Apache Hadoop is the de facto distributed data operating system, managing a variety of resources, data and computing tasks across clusters of commodity hardware.

questions.q: When a client writes a file to HDFS, after it contacts the NameNode, the NameNode responds with:
o: the IP addresses of the DataNodes (e.g. 3 of them) where the replicas will be stored
questions.e: On a write, the NameNode does not store actual data; it replies with the IP addresses of (by default 3) DataNodes where the replicas will be stored. The client then writes to the first DataNode.

questions.q: During an HDFS write, data flows through the DataNodes in what is called a:
o: write pipeline (DN1 forwards to DN2, which forwards to DN3)
questions.e: During a write, the client writes the block to the first DataNode, which forwards it to the second, which forwards it to the third — this chain is called the write pipeline. Acknowledgements then flow back up the pipeline.

questions.q: In an HDFS write, after all three DataNodes store the block and acknowledgements flow back, the client then:
o: sends a 'Write Successful' message to the NameNode, which updates its metadata
questions.e: Once the client receives ACKs from all three DataNodes, it sends a 'Write Successful' message to the NameNode, which updates its metadata (recording that the block is stored on those DataNodes).

questions.q: During an HDFS read, after the NameNode returns the DataNode locations, the client:
o: connects directly to the DataNodes to fetch the blocks (not via the NameNode)
reads all data through the NameNode
re-asks the NameNode for each byte
questions.e: On a read, the NameNode returns a list of DataNodes holding copies of the required blocks; the client then connects directly to the DataNodes to fetch blocks (not via the NameNode) and assembles them in the correct order.

questions.q: A key HDFS design principle regarding the NameNode is that:
o: the NameNode stores all data blocks
clients always read/write data through the NameNode
clients never read or write file data through the NameNode — the NameNode only tells clients which DataNodes to contact
questions.e: HDFS is designed so clients never read and write file data through the NameNode; a client asks the NameNode which DataNodes to contact (via ClientProtocol over RPC), then communicates directly with a DataNode using the DataTransferProtocol.

questions.q: In classic Hadoop (Hadoop 1.0), the master daemon that handled both job coordination and resource allocation for MapReduce was the:
questions.e: In Hadoop 1.0, the JobTracker (on the master) handled both job coordination and resource allocation; the TaskTrackers (on slave nodes) just executed the tasks (Map or Reduce) assigned to them.

questions.q: In classic Hadoop, the per-node agent on slave machines that executes Map or Reduce tasks is the:
questions.e: The TaskTracker is the per-node agent on slave machines that executes tasks (Map or Reduce) on the data; each slave machine usually runs both a DataNode (storage) and a TaskTracker (processing).

questions.q: In Hadoop's server roles, the master nodes include the NameNode, the Secondary NameNode, and the ______, while slave nodes run the DataNode and ______.
questions.e: Master nodes: NameNode (HDFS boss), Secondary NameNode (helper), and JobTracker (processing boss). Slave nodes: DataNode (stores data blocks) and TaskTracker (executes tasks).

questions.q: The difference between an Active NameNode and a Standby NameNode is that:
o: the active NameNode handles client requests and manages the file system, while the standby stays ready to take over (a backup that synchronizes its state)
questions.e: The active NameNode actively handles client requests and manages the file system (the primary authority for metadata), while the standby NameNode remains in standby mode as a backup, synchronizing its state, ready to take over.

questions.q: A Hadoop Cluster is:
o: a group of many computers (nodes) connected through a network, working together to store and process huge amounts of data
questions.e: A Hadoop Cluster is a group of many computers (nodes) connected through a network, working together to store and process huge amounts of data; nodes are grouped into racks connected by switches.

questions.q: The typical Hadoop workflow is:
o: load data into HDFS → analyze with MapReduce → store results in HDFS → read results from HDFS
questions.e: The typical workflow is: load data into the cluster (HDFS writes) → analyze the data (MapReduce) → store results in the cluster (HDFS writes) → read the results from the cluster (HDFS reads).

questions.q: A 300 MB file stored in HDFS with a block size of 128 MB will be divided into how many blocks?
questions.e: A 300 MB file with 128 MB block size is divided into 3 blocks: 128 MB + 128 MB + 44 MB. With a replication factor of 3, there would be 9 total block copies across the cluster.

questions.q: The Secondary NameNode connects to the NameNode (by default) approximately:
o: every hour (configurable) to do housekeeping and back up metadata
questions.e: The Secondary NameNode is not a hot standby; it connects to the NameNode every hour (configurable) for housekeeping and to back up NameNode metadata, and the saved metadata can help rebuild a failed NameNode.

questions.q: In the Hadoop processing workflow, after the client submits a job, the JobTracker:
o: divides the job into tasks and sends them to TaskTrackers located close to the DataNodes where the data resides
questions.e: The JobTracker divides the job into tasks and sends them to TaskTrackers (close to the DataNodes where the data resides); each TaskTracker processes its portion in parallel, and results are combined and returned to the client.

questions.q: In the master-worker pattern used by MapReduce, communication occurs:
o: only between the master process and the worker processes (no direct worker-to-worker communication)
questions.e: In the master-worker pattern, the master manages assignments to workers and workers execute assigned tasks; communication occurs only between the master and the workers — no direct worker-to-worker communication is possible.

questions.q: MapReduce is best described as:
o: a data-parallel programming model for clusters of commodity machines, pioneered by Google
questions.e: MapReduce is a data-parallel programming model for clusters of commodity machines, pioneered by Google (which could process >20 PB per day) and popularized by the open-source Hadoop project.

questions.q: A MapReduce program is composed of two procedures: Map() and Reduce(). Their roles are:
o: Map performs a transformation; Reduce performs a summarization (aggregation) operation
Map performs summarization; Reduce performs transformation
questions.e: A MapReduce program has a Map() procedure that performs a transformation (processing a key-value pair into intermediate key-value pairs) and a Reduce() procedure that performs a summarization/aggregation (combining all intermediate values for the same key).

questions.q: The Map function in MapReduce processes a key-value pair and generates:
o: a set of intermediate key-value pairs
questions.e: The user-defined Map function processes an input key-value pair and generates a set of intermediate key-value pairs; the Reduce function then aggregates all intermediate values associated with the same intermediate key.

questions.q: In the MapReduce 'Shuffle & Sort' step, the system:
o: sends each intermediate result to the right reducer and groups/sorts the values by key (e.g. (cat,1),(cat,1) → (cat,[1,1]))
questions.e: In the Shuffle & Sort step, intermediate results from all workers are shuffled (sent to the right reducer) and sorted/grouped by key — e.g. (cat,1),(cat,1),(dog,1) becomes (cat,[1,1]),(dog,[1]).

questions.q: MPI (Message Passing Interface) is not well-suited for big data because:
o: it only runs on one machine
it focuses on computation/communication but does not handle data distribution and I/O well, which are critical for big data
it is too easy to use
questions.e: MPI provides a comprehensive API for data transfer and synchronization and is used in supercomputers/scientific computing, but it mainly focuses on computation and inter-process communication and almost ignores data distribution and I/O, which are critical for big data — so Google invented MapReduce.

questions.q: A 'shared-nothing' architecture means that:
o: every node works independently with its own CPU, RAM, disk and OS, communicating only through the network
all nodes share one memory and disk
questions.e: Shared-nothing architecture means every node works independently and does not share its memory (RAM) or storage (disk) with other nodes; each node has its own CPU, RAM, storage and OS, and nodes communicate through the network. This makes systems easy to scale and fault-tolerant.

questions.q: In MapReduce, the number of Mappers Hadoop creates is determined by:
o: the number of input splits (No. of Mappers = No. of Input Splits)
questions.e: The number of Mappers is determined by the number of Input Splits in the data: No. of Mappers = No. of Input Splits. You control it by controlling the number of input splits (e.g. via the 'mapred.max.split.size' property).

questions.q: In MapReduce, mappers save their outputs to ______ rather than pushing them directly to reducers, which allows recovery if a reducer crashes.
questions.e: Mappers save their outputs to local disk rather than pushing them directly to reducers, which allows recovery if a reducer crashes; the output of reducers is then stored in HDFS (and may be replicated).

questions.q: In a 'single reduce task' MapReduce job:
o: only one reducer runs after all mappers finish, combining everything into a single output file — simple but slow for huge data
each mapper has its own reducer
questions.e: With a single reduce task, only one reducer runs after all mappers finish; all intermediate results are sent to it and combined into a single output file (e.g. part-0). It is simple and good for small/moderate data, but slow for huge data.

questions.q: In a 'no reduce task' MapReduce job:
o: the reduce phase is completely skipped, and the map output directly becomes the final output — used for transformation or filtering
questions.e: In a 'no reduce task' scenario, the reduce phase is completely skipped and the output of each mapper directly becomes the final output; it is used when you only need to transform or filter data (e.g. filtering logs for lines containing 'ERROR'), not aggregate.

questions.q: How does MapReduce handle a 'straggler' (a task running slowly)?
o: it launches a second copy of the task on another node and takes the output of whichever copy finishes first (speculative execution)
questions.e: For a straggler (slow task), MapReduce launches a second copy of the task on another node and takes the output of whichever copy finishes first, killing the other — this speculative execution is critical for performance in large clusters where stragglers occur frequently.

questions.q: If a task crashes in MapReduce, the system:
o: retries the task on another node (okay for map since it has no dependencies, okay for reduce since map outputs are on disk)
questions.e: If a task crashes, MapReduce retries it on another node; this is okay for a map task (no dependencies) and for a reduce task (map outputs are on disk). If the same task repeatedly fails, the job can fail or that input block can be ignored (user-controlled).

questions.q: In a shared-nothing distributed environment, MapReduce makes computation efficient by:
o: moving all data to one central node
executing the computation near the data it operates on (migrating computation closer to the data), minimizing network traffic
questions.e: In a shared-nothing environment, a computation is much more efficient if executed near the data it operates on; when the dataset is huge, migrating the computation closer to the data minimizes network traffic and increases overall throughput.

questions.q: The MapReduce environment automatically takes care of which of the following?
o: partitioning input data, scheduling execution, the group-by-key (shuffle/sort), handling machine failures and inter-machine communication
questions.e: The MapReduce environment automatically handles partitioning the input data, scheduling execution across machines, performing the group-by-key step in Shuffle and Sort, handling machine failures, and managing inter-machine communication — so the user focuses on the application.

questions.q: In MapReduce execution, the Job Tracker monitors the status of Task Trackers through:
questions.e: The Job Tracker monitors Task Trackers' status through heartbeat signals; on a Task Tracker failure, it reassigns tasks and selects replicas for data retrieval.

questions.q: A principal philosophy of MapReduce is to:
o: make it scale (throw hardware at problems) and make it cheap (commodity hardware, requiring fault tolerance)
questions.e: MapReduce's principal philosophies are: make it scale, so you can throw hardware at problems; and make it cheap, saving hardware, programmer and administration costs (which requires fault tolerance). It is not suitable for all problems, but can save a lot of time when it works.

questions.q: In MapReduce, the mappers are preferentially placed:
o: on the same node or same rack as their input block (push computation to data, minimize network use)
on a random node far from the data
questions.e: Mappers are preferentially placed on the same node or same rack as their input block — pushing computation to the data to minimize network use.

questions.q: Benefits of the MapReduce data-parallel programming model include:
o: manual job division and manual failure recovery
automatic division of jobs into tasks, automatic placement of computation near data, automatic load balancing, and recovery from failures and stragglers
questions.e: MapReduce provides automatic division of a job into tasks, automatic placement of computation near data, automatic load balancing, and recovery from failures and stragglers — so the user focuses on the application, not the complexities of distributed computing.

questions.q: The 'coordinator' (master node) in MapReduce is responsible for:
o: executing all map and reduce functions itself
scheduling map/reduce tasks, tracking task status (idle, in-progress, completed), managing intermediate file locations, and pinging workers to detect failures
questions.e: The master node coordinates: it tracks task status (idle/in-progress/completed), schedules idle tasks on available workers, forwards intermediate file locations from completed map tasks to reducers, and periodically pings workers to detect failures.

questions.q: YARN stands for:
questions.e: YARN stands for 'Yet Another Resource Negotiator'; it is the resource management and job scheduling framework introduced in Hadoop 2.0.

questions.q: In Hadoop 1.0, a fundamental limitation was that:
o: MapReduce was also the resource manager, so a cluster could only run one application type (usually a MapReduce batch job) at a time
questions.e: In Hadoop 1.0, MapReduce was not just a processing model but also the resource manager; the JobTracker handled both job coordination and resource allocation, so each cluster could run only one application type at a time — usually a large MapReduce batch job.

questions.q: YARN was introduced in Hadoop 2.0 primarily to:
o: remove the bottleneck on the JobTracker that existed in Hadoop 1.0, and take Hadoop beyond batch processing
questions.e: YARN is the resource management and job scheduling framework in Hadoop 2.0, introduced to remove the bottleneck on the JobTracker present in Hadoop 1.0 and to take Hadoop beyond batch (supporting streaming, interactive, graph processing, etc.).

questions.q: The fundamental idea of YARN is to split the two major functions of the old JobTracker into:
o: cluster resource management (ResourceManager) and application life-cycle management (ApplicationMaster)
questions.e: YARN splits the JobTracker's two functions: cluster resource management goes to the ResourceManager, and application life-cycle management goes to a per-application ApplicationMaster. MapReduce becomes just a user-land library (one of many apps).

questions.q: Under YARN, MapReduce becomes:
o: a user-land library — one of many applications (like Spark, Flink) that can run on top of YARN
questions.e: With YARN, MapReduce is no longer tightly integrated into Hadoop's core; it becomes a user-land library that runs on top of a YARN-managed cluster alongside other applications like Spark, Flink or custom ones.

questions.q: In YARN, the master daemon responsible for resource assignment and management among all applications is the:
questions.e: The ResourceManager is the master daemon of YARN; it receives job submissions, decides which node runs which task and how much CPU/memory each gets, and optimizes cluster utilization. It has two internal parts: the Scheduler and the Application Manager.

questions.q: The YARN ResourceManager's Scheduler is a 'pure scheduler', meaning it:
o: only allocates resources to applications based on their requirements, and does NOT monitor status or restart failed tasks
questions.e: The Scheduler is a pure scheduler in the ResourceManager: it allocates resources to running applications subject to capacity/queue constraints, but it does not monitor or track application status, and does not guarantee restarting failed tasks.

questions.q: The three schedulers available in YARN are:
questions.e: Three schedulers are available in YARN: FIFO, the Capacity Scheduler, and the Fair Scheduler.

questions.q: The FIFO scheduler works by:
o: dividing the cluster into fixed queues
placing jobs in a queue by arrival order, giving the first job all cluster resources until it finishes before the next job starts
redistributing resources as new jobs arrive
giving all jobs an equal share
questions.e: FIFO (First-In-First-Out): jobs are queued by arrival order; the first job gets all cluster resources until it finishes, and the next job waits — like a line at a ticket counter. It is simple but slows down smaller/newer jobs.

questions.q: The Capacity Scheduler is designed for multi-tenant clusters and works by:
o: dividing the cluster into multiple queues, each with a fixed/minimum capacity, where idle capacity can be temporarily borrowed
redistributing resources equally at all times
questions.e: The Capacity Scheduler is designed for multi-tenant clusters shared by multiple teams: the cluster is divided into queues each with a fixed or minimum guaranteed capacity, and if one queue is idle, another can temporarily use its capacity.

questions.q: The Fair Scheduler works by:
o: serving the first job completely first
giving all jobs an equal share of resources over time (one job can use the full cluster; when a new job arrives, resources are divided fairly)
questions.e: The Fair Scheduler is designed for fairness and responsiveness: all jobs get an equal share of resources over time; if only one job runs it can use the full cluster, and when a new job arrives resources are redistributed fairly (e.g. 50-50).

questions.q: In YARN, the per-machine agent that reports node health/resources to the ResourceManager and launches/monitors containers is the:
questions.e: The NodeManager runs on each machine (node); it registers with the ResourceManager, sends heartbeats with the node's health status, and launches and monitors the containers (where actual work happens) assigned to it.

questions.q: In YARN, the ApplicationMaster is:
o: the master daemon for the whole cluster
a per-application entity (started in a container by the ResourceManager) that negotiates resources, requests containers, and tracks the progress of that one application
questions.e: Each application (job) has its own ApplicationMaster — a framework-specific entity started by the ResourceManager inside a container; it negotiates resources from the ResourceManager, works with NodeManagers to execute/monitor tasks, and reports progress.

questions.q: In YARN, a 'Container' is:
o: a collection of physical resources (RAM, CPU cores, disk) on a single node, granting an application the right to use a specific amount of resources
questions.e: A Container is a collection of physical resources (RAM, CPU cores, disks) on a single node; it grants an application the right to use a specific amount of resources on a specific host. Each Map or Reduce task runs inside a separate container.

questions.q: The NodeManager launches a container when it receives a ______ from the ApplicationMaster.
o: Container Launch Context (CLC), which includes everything the application needs to run
questions.e: The ApplicationMaster requests the assigned container from the NodeManager by sending it a Container Launch Context (CLC), which includes everything the application needs to run; the NodeManager then creates and starts the container process.

questions.q: Which of the following is an enhancement/benefit that YARN brings to a Hadoop cluster?
o: scalability, compatibility (supports existing MapReduce apps), better cluster utilization, and multi-tenancy
questions.e: YARN enhances Hadoop with scalability (manage thousands of nodes), compatibility (supports existing MapReduce apps without disruption), cluster utilization (dynamic utilization), and multi-tenancy (multiple engine access).

questions.q: In the YARN application workflow, the first step after a client submits an application is that the ResourceManager:
o: allocates a container to start the Application Master, which then registers with the ResourceManager
questions.e: In the YARN workflow: the client submits an application; the ResourceManager allocates a container to start the ApplicationMaster; the ApplicationMaster registers with the ResourceManager, then requests containers, notifies NodeManagers to launch them, and the application code executes in the containers.

questions.q: A stated limitation of classic MapReduce (MapReduce v1) is that:
o: iterative algorithms (common in machine learning) are about 10x slower because data must be read/written to disk between iterations
questions.e: Classic MapReduce has high latency and no built-in optimization for iterative algorithms: iterative applications implemented in MapReduce are about 10x slower because of repeated disk reads/writes between iterations; it also has scalability limits (max ~4000 nodes, 40000 concurrent tasks) and is not suited to real-time processing.

questions.q: In the YARN ResourceManager, the 'Application Manager' component is responsible for:
o: accepting job submissions and negotiating the first container from the ResourceManager to run the application-specific ApplicationMaster
questions.e: The Application Manager (within the ResourceManager) accepts job submissions, negotiates the first container for executing the application-specific ApplicationMaster, and manages/restarts ApplicationMasters on failure. (The Scheduler separately allocates resources to running jobs.)

questions.q: Micro-batch processing is best described as:
o: processing each record instantly with sub-second latency
running batch processes on much smaller accumulations of data (typically less than a minute's worth), giving near-real-time results
questions.e: Micro-batch processing runs batch processes on much smaller accumulations of data (typically less than a minute's worth), so data is available in near real-time; in practice there is little difference between micro-batching and stream processing.

questions.q: Three workloads that MapReduce struggled with — prompting Spark — were complex multi-pass algorithms, interactive ad-hoc queries, and:
questions.e: MapReduce was great for batch processing, but users needed more: complex multi-pass algorithms, interactive ad-hoc queries, and real-time stream processing — leading to specialized systems and ultimately to Spark.

questions.q: All three workloads that MapReduce struggled with share a need for one thing that MapReduce lacks:
questions.e: Although complex algorithms, interactive queries and stream processing look different, all three need one thing MapReduce lacks: efficient data sharing. Spark provides this (keeping data in memory).

questions.q: A problem with using many specialized systems (one for batch, one for streaming, etc.) is that:
o: there are more systems to manage/tune/deploy, you can't easily combine processing types, and data transfer between engines can dominate cost
questions.e: With specialized systems, there are more systems to manage, tune and deploy; you can't easily combine processing types (even though most apps need to, e.g. load with SQL then run ML), and data transfer between engines is often a dominant cost.

questions.q: Spark is described as a 'unified engine' because it:
o: can only run on one machine
combines batch, SQL, streaming, machine learning and graph processing into one platform
questions.e: Spark combines many tasks into one engine: Spark Core (batch), Spark SQL (SQL queries), Spark Streaming/Structured Streaming (streaming), MLlib (machine learning) and GraphX (graph processing) — a unified engine instead of many separate systems.

questions.q: RDD stands for:
questions.e: RDD stands for Resilient Distributed Dataset, a fundamental concept in Apache Spark — a fault-tolerant collection of elements that can be operated on in parallel.

questions.q: In 'Resilient Distributed Dataset', the 'Resilient' part means RDDs:
o: can recover from failures by rebuilding lost partitions
questions.e: RDDs are resilient because they can recover from failures: if part of an RDD is lost due to hardware failure, it can rebuild itself — like picking up a dropped puzzle piece and continuing.

questions.q: Spark achieves its resilience (ability to rebuild lost data) by:
o: copying all data to disk constantly
tracking lineage information — the sequence of transformations used to build each RDD — so lost data can be recomputed
asking the user to re-enter data
questions.e: Spark keeps track of the steps (lineage) it takes to process data; if something goes wrong, it can redo those steps to rebuild the original data state — like using written-down baking steps to remake a dropped cake.

questions.q: Spark is generally much faster than Hadoop MapReduce primarily because Spark:
o: can cache/keep data in memory between operations, avoiding repeated disk reads/writes (especially for iterative/interactive workloads)
questions.e: Spark can cache data in memory, keeping frequently accessed data in RAM so multiple processing steps don't need to re-read from disk; this makes it much faster than Hadoop MapReduce, which reads/writes to disk at each step, especially for iterative or interactive workloads.

questions.q: The key difference between Hadoop MapReduce and Spark in how they process data is:
o: Hadoop is in-memory; Spark is disk-based
Hadoop MapReduce is batch-oriented (disk-based), while Spark can process in real-time and in-memory, making it much faster
questions.e: Hadoop MapReduce processes data in a batch-oriented, disk-based manner, while Spark can process data in real-time and in-memory, making it much faster — able to update analysis as new data arrives without reloading the entire dataset.

questions.q: Before Spark, companies had to use many different tools; which tool was used for stream processing?
questions.e: Before Spark: MapReduce → batch processing, Storm → stream processing, Giraph/Pregel → graph processing, Impala/Presto → SQL queries, Mahout → machine learning. Spark unifies these into one engine.

questions.q: The RDD programming model builds RDDs via:
o: parallel transformations (map, filter, …) on collections of objects stored in RAM or disk across the cluster
questions.e: In the Spark programming model, RDDs are collections of objects stored in RAM or disk across the cluster, built via parallel transformations (map, filter, …), automatically rebuilt on failure, and they track lineage info to rebuild lost data.

questions.q: When is batch processing a good choice (vs stream)?
o: when data arrives one record at a time at high velocity
when data freshness is not mission-critical and you are running complex algorithms needing the entire batch (e.g. sorting the whole dataset)
questions.e: Batch processing suits cases where data freshness is not mission-critical, you work with large datasets needing the entire batch (e.g. sorting), you get data in batches, or you join tables in relational databases.

questions.q: When is stream processing the right choice?
o: when results can wait a day
when data freshness is super-important, data arrives continuously at high velocity, and sub-second latency is crucial
questions.e: Stream processing is used where data freshness is super-important, data is generated in a continuous high-velocity stream, and sub-second latency is crucial (e.g. detecting anomalies in machinery, live fraud detection).

questions.q: Recent additions to Spark include a DataFrame API (similar to R and Pandas), an R interface, and:
questions.e: Recent Spark additions include the DataFrame API (similar to R and Pandas) for structured data, SparkR (an R interface), and machine learning pipelines (like Scikit-learn) for developing/deploying ML workflows.

questions.q: Spark's goal, compared with specialized systems, was to:
o: build a separate engine for each workload
generalize MapReduce to support new applications within the same engine
questions.e: Unlike the various specialized systems, Spark's goal was to generalize MapReduce to support new apps within the same engine, using two small additions: fast data sharing and general DAGs.

questions.q: The two reasonably small additions that let Spark generalize MapReduce are:
o: fast data sharing and general DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs)
questions.e: Spark generalizes MapReduce with two additions: fast data sharing and general DAGs. By supporting general DAGs, Spark can represent iterative algorithms, ML pipelines and graph processing efficiently.

questions.q: In Spark, a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is used to:
o: show all operations and their dependencies so Spark can plan the most efficient route to the final result
questions.e: Instead of running each step immediately, Spark builds a DAG showing all operations and their dependencies; it uses this to plan the most efficient route to compute the final result (reusing steps, avoiding repetition).

questions.q: SparkContext is best described as:
o: the main entry point to Spark functionality — the connection between your application and the Spark cluster
questions.e: SparkContext is the main entry point for Spark functionality; it is the first object a Spark program creates, tells Spark how to access a cluster, and is used to create RDDs, accumulators and broadcast variables. Only one SparkContext should be active per JVM.

questions.q: In the SparkContext master parameter, 'local[K]' means:
o: run Spark on your own computer using K parallel threads (e.g. local[4] uses 4 CPU cores)
questions.e: The master parameter determines the cluster: 'local' runs on one CPU core (no parallelism), 'local[K]' runs with K parallel threads (e.g. local[4] = 4 cores), 'spark://HOST:PORT' connects to a Spark cluster, and 'mesos://HOST:PORT' connects to a Mesos cluster.

questions.q: In Spark's architecture, the 'Driver' is:
o: the 'brain'/control center where the application starts; it divides work into tasks, distributes data, manages resources, and collects results
questions.e: The Driver is like the brain of a Spark application: it is where the app starts, divides work into tasks and sends them to worker nodes, decides data distribution, manages resources, and collects/aggregates the final results.

questions.q: In Spark's architecture, an 'Executor' is:
o: a worker that runs on each worker node, executing tasks in parallel and managing its own CPU/memory
questions.e: An Executor runs on each worker node; when the Driver sends tasks, each is executed by an Executor (filtering, calculations, joins). Executors process data in parallel, manage their own resources, and handle failures (Spark reruns lost tasks on other executors).

questions.q: The two types of operations on RDDs are:
questions.e: There are two types of operations on RDDs: transformations (which create a new RDD from an existing one and are lazy) and actions (which trigger computation and return raw values).

questions.q: RDD transformations in Spark are 'lazy', which means:
o: they are not computed right away — Spark remembers them and only computes when an action is called
questions.e: All transformations in Spark are lazy: they do not compute results right away but remember the transformations applied to a base dataset, letting Spark optimize the calculations and recover lost partitions. They only execute when an action is called.

questions.q: Which of the following is an RDD transformation?
o: map (applies a function to each element, returning a new RDD)
questions.e: Transformations create a new RDD from an existing one; examples include map (apply a function to each element), filter (keep elements meeting a condition), reduce, and flatMap. (collect, count, first are actions.)

questions.q: Which of the following is an RDD action?
o: collect() (gathers all elements back to the driver)
questions.e: Actions trigger actual computation and return raw values (not a new RDD); examples include collect() (gather all elements to the driver), count(), first(), take(n) and reduce(). An action sends data from the executors to the driver.

questions.q: A defining feature of an RDD action (versus a transformation) is that it:
o: returns a value other than an RDD (the raw result), and does not form a new RDD
questions.e: Any RDD function that returns something other than RDD[T] is considered an action; actions do not form new RDDs — their values are stored to the driver or to external storage, and they are one of the ways of sending data from executors to the driver.

questions.q: Persistence (caching) in Spark is used to:
o: cache/store RDDs in memory or on disk across operations to avoid recomputing them each time they are used
questions.e: Persistence refers to caching/storing RDDs in memory or on disk across multiple operations to avoid recomputation; by persisting in memory, Spark can make future actions more than 10x faster, using persist() or cache() (and unpersist() to release).

questions.q: Spark's cache is fault-tolerant because:
o: if any partition of an RDD is lost, it is automatically recomputed using the transformations (lineage) that originally created it
questions.e: Spark can persist a dataset in memory across operations, making future actions 10x+ faster; the cache is fault-tolerant because if any partition of an RDD is lost, it will automatically be recomputed using the transformations that originally created it.

questions.q: Spark SQL is a component that:
o: provides a programming interface for working with structured data, letting users query data using SQL (working with DataFrames under the hood)
questions.e: Spark SQL provides a programming interface for structured data, enabling SQL queries (or Python/Scala/Java) on data sources like RDDs, DataFrames and Hive; under the hood it works with DataFrames (like tables with rows and columns) and optimizes queries for parallel execution.

questions.q: Spark MLlib is:
o: a scalable machine learning library built on Spark, with algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, collaborative filtering and dimensionality reduction
questions.e: Spark MLlib is a scalable machine learning library built on Apache Spark; it includes algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, collaborative filtering and dimensionality reduction, distributing computations across a cluster for big data.

questions.q: Spark MLlib uses which structure as its input data for algorithms?
o: DataFrames (an alias of Dataset<Row>) — i.e. structured, tabular data
questions.e: Spark MLlib uses DataFrames (an alias of Dataset<Row>) as input; the input must be represented as 'tables' before applying MLlib algorithms, with columns such as 'label' (target) and 'features' (a vector of attribute values).

questions.q: In Spark MLlib, a 'Pipeline':
o: chains multiple Transformers and Estimators together to specify a machine learning/data-mining workflow, where each stage's output feeds the next
questions.e: A Pipeline chains multiple Transformers and Estimators together to specify an ML/data-mining workflow; the output of each transformer/estimator is the input of the next (e.g. split documents into words → convert to feature vectors → learn a model).

questions.q: In Spark MLlib, a Transformer and an Estimator are respectively:
o: a storage format and a network protocol
a component that transforms one Dataset<Row> into another; and a component that builds (fits) an ML model from training data
questions.e: A Transformer is an ML algorithm/procedure that transforms one Dataset<Row> into another (e.g. converting text to numerical vectors, scaling features). An Estimator is a component used to build ML models — a blueprint for creating a model from training data.

questions.q: Spark Streaming processes live data by:
o: processing each byte individually with no batching
waiting a full day before processing
running the streaming computation as a series of very small, deterministic batch jobs (splitting the stream into batches of X seconds)
questions.e: Spark Streaming runs a streaming computation as a series of very small, deterministic batch jobs; it splits the live stream into batches of X seconds, treats each batch as RDDs, processes them with RDD operations, and returns results in batches.

questions.q: In Spark Streaming, a DStream (Discretized Stream) is:
o: a continuous stream of data divided into small, discrete batches, each represented as a sequence of RDDs
questions.e: A DStream (Discretized Stream) represents a continuous stream of data divided into small, discrete fixed-duration micro-batches; each batch is an immutable RDD, enabling fault tolerance (lost RDDs can be recomputed) and familiar batch operations (map, reduce, window, join).

questions.q: Spark GraphX is a component for:
o: processing and analyzing graph data (nodes and edges) in a distributed manner, with algorithms like PageRank, Triangle Count, Shortest Paths and Connected Components
questions.e: Spark GraphX processes and analyzes graph data (nodes = entities, edges = relationships) across a cluster; built-in algorithms include PageRank, Personalized PageRank, Triangle Count, Shortest Paths, Connected Components, Strongly Connected Components and Label Propagation.

questions.q: The two types of RDDs you can create in Spark are:
o: parallelized collections (from an existing collection) and Hadoop datasets (from files in HDFS or other Hadoop-supported storage)
questions.e: Two types of RDDs: parallelized collections — take an existing collection and run functions on it in parallel; and Hadoop datasets — run functions on each record of a file in HDFS or any other storage supported by Hadoop (local FS, Amazon S3, HBase, etc.).

questions.q: In the Hadoop setup labs, Docker is used because:
o: it is a container platform that lets you run Hadoop easily without complex manual installation, packaging everything together and running consistently anywhere
questions.e: Docker is a container platform used to run Hadoop easily, avoiding complex manual installation; a Docker container packages the application plus its dependencies and runs the same on a laptop, lab PC or server (like a lunchbox that tastes the same everywhere).

questions.q: WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is needed in the setup because it:
o: provides a Linux environment inside Windows, which is required for Docker to run Linux containers
questions.e: WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) provides a Linux environment inside Windows and is required for Docker to run Linux containers (and thus Hadoop); it can be installed with 'wsl --install'.

questions.q: Which command pulls the Hadoop NameNode container image?
questions.e: The NameNode image is pulled with 'docker pull bde2020/hadoop-namenode' (it manages metadata — files, directories, blocks); the DataNode image is 'docker pull bde2020/hadoop-datanode' (stores actual data blocks).

questions.q: Which command creates the virtual Docker network that lets Hadoop nodes communicate?
questions.e: 'docker network create hadoop' creates a virtual network allowing communication between the NameNode and DataNode containers by hostname, mimicking a real distributed environment.

questions.q: The HDFS command 'hdfs dfs -ls' is used to:
o: check the replication factor of one file
list files in HDFS (showing permissions, size and replication)
questions.e: 'hdfs dfs -ls' lists files in HDFS, displaying permissions, size and replication. ('hdfs dfsadmin -report' shows cluster status/health, and 'hdfs dfs -stat %r <file>' checks a file's replication factor.)

questions.q: The command 'hdfs dfsadmin -report' is used to:
o: display cluster status/health — DataNodes, storage and usage
questions.e: 'hdfs dfsadmin -report' performs a cluster health check, displaying cluster status including the DataNodes, storage and usage.

questions.q: To check the replication factor of a specific file in HDFS, you use:
questions.e: 'hdfs dfs -stat %r <file>' checks the replication factor of a file, which ensures fault tolerance.

questions.q: The command 'docker ps' is used to:
o: verify which containers are running (e.g. the namenode plus multiple datanodes)
questions.e: 'docker ps' checks running containers, verifying that all containers (expected: namenode + multiple datanodes) are running.

questions.q: In the MapReduce Docker lab, the example job that was run to verify the Hadoop cluster was a:
o: Word-Count MapReduce job (tokenizing lines into words, emitting <word, 1>, then summing counts)
questions.e: The lab ran a Word-Count MapReduce job: each line was tokenized into words, each word emitted as <word, 1>; Hadoop then shuffled/sorted to group identical words, and reducers summed the counts (e.g. 'is' → 2), writing the output to HDFS.

questions.q: In the Docker lab, uploading a local file into HDFS is done with the command:
questions.e: The file was uploaded into HDFS using 'hdfs dfs -put /tmp/data.txt /input'; HDFS then stored the file under /input/data.txt. The MapReduce job read from /input and wrote results to /output.

questions.q: Power BI is:
o: a Microsoft business intelligence and data visualization tool used for analyzing and visualizing data
questions.e: Power BI is a Microsoft business intelligence and data visualization tool used for analyzing and visualizing data, creating interactive dashboards and reports — popular for data analytics and business reporting.

questions.q: In Power BI, data (such as Excel or CSV files) is imported using the:
questions.e: In Power BI you import Excel or CSV files using the 'Get Data' option, select and load datasets, and can preview data before importing.

questions.q: The three main views in Power BI Desktop are:
o: Map View, Chart View and Table View
Edit View, Print View and Save View
Report View, Data View and Model View
Batch View, Stream View and Micro View
questions.e: Power BI Desktop has a Report View (for creating visuals), a Data View (for viewing tables), and a Model View (for relationships); the Visualization and Fields panes are on the right.

questions.q: In Power BI, the Model View is used for:
questions.e: In Power BI Desktop, the Report View is for creating visuals, the Data View is for viewing tables, and the Model View is for defining relationships between tables.

questions.q: A key interactive feature of Power BI reports is that:
o: clicking one chart automatically filters the other charts, making analysis dynamic and interactive
charts must be refreshed manually every time
only one chart is allowed per report
questions.e: Power BI charts interact automatically: clicking one chart filters the others, making analysis dynamic and interactive — useful for business insights.

questions.q: To create a chart in Power BI, you typically:
o: select a visualization type and drag fields into the chart areas, then customize titles and formatting
questions.e: To create your first chart in Power BI, you select a visualization type, drag fields into the chart areas (e.g. to create bar or column charts), and customize titles and formatting.

questions.q: Power BI reports are saved as which file type?
questions.e: Power BI reports are saved as .pbix files; they can be published to the Power BI Service, shared with others, and accessed online.

questions.q: After creating a report in Power BI, you can share it with others by:
o: publishing the report to the Power BI Service and sharing the dashboard online
questions.e: You save reports as .pbix files, then publish reports to the Power BI Service to share dashboards with others and access reports online.

questions.q: Power BI's AI Insights feature helps users by:
o: providing AI-based insights to quickly identify patterns and trends with automatic analysis features
questions.e: Power BI provides AI-based insights that quickly identify patterns and trends, with automatic analysis features that are helpful for beginners and analysts.
